title: Day 69 · Week 9, Day 6 — Myths: boy or girl — the heartbeat over a hundred and forty, the basketball bump, the lunar calendar tested on 2.8 million births, timing and cereal, the ring on a thread, and the one piece of folklore that is partly true
summary: The sex-prediction folklore, each myth against the study that tested it. Where your baby is: Carnegie stage 23, ~30 mm, the last day of the embryonic period, with SRY switching the gonads at 6–7 weeks post-fertilization and the external anatomy not yet readable. The sex ratio at conception is 0.5 (Orzack 2015), so every method is right half the time. Heart rate: no sex difference in 212 pregnancies across 2,261 visits (Genuis 1996) or in 477 first-trimester scans (girls 151.7 vs boys 154.9 bpm; McKenna 2006) — it tracks age, not sex. Bump shape and morning-sickness folklore failed in 104 women (Perry 1999), and maternal intuition was no better than chance (Genuis 1996). The Chinese lunar calendar on 2,840,755 Swedish births: kappa 0.0002 (Villamor 2010). Timing of intercourse made no difference (Wilcox 1995, NEJM). The breakfast-cereal finding (Mathews 2008) was most likely a multiple-testing false positive (Young 2009). The ring on a thread, urine chemistry (and the drain-cleaner hazard) and the six-week placenta method have no published validation. The partly true one: severe sickness is linked to girls (54.1% vs 48.7% overall; Mitsuda 2019; Askling 1999) — a real association and still a nearly useless predictor.
action: For fun: tonight each of you writes a boy/girl guess and the method behind it (heartbeat, bump, dream, calendar, a real coin toss); add two grandparents' guesses and methods. Seal them in an envelope dated Day 69, put it in the back of the Day 61 pregnancy file, and open it the day you find out.
